title: ZLIB Compressed Data Format Specification version 3.3
summary: Defines the zlib compressed data format, a lossless format that wraps compressed data with a small header and checksum. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: zlib wraps compressed bytes with information that identifies the compression method and checks the recovered data. This RFC specifies the wrapper and its Adler-32 checksum.

questions: what is a zlib preset dictionary
how does the zlib header work
subtitle: The zlib wrapper for compressed data, including its header, optional dictionary identifier, and Adler-32 checksum.

tldr.problem: Software needs a lossless compressed-data format that works across computer systems and can process a sequential stream using bounded intermediate storage.
tldr.mechanism: A zlib stream contains a two-byte header, optional dictionary identifier, compressed data, and an Adler-32 checksum of the uncompressed data. This version uses DEFLATE as its compression method.
tldr.outcome: The format detects some data corruption through its checksum. A decompressor that does not check the checksum may allow corruption to go undetected.

today: RFC 1950 is an Informational RFC published in May 1996, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document states that it does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Goals and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1950 specifies a lossless compressed-data format intended to be independent of CPU type, operating system, file system, and character set. It can process an arbitrarily long sequential input stream using a bounded amount of intermediate storage.

The format does not provide random access to compressed data. Its scope is in-memory compression of a sequence of arbitrary bytes, and it can be extended to use other compression methods.
sections.plainLanguage: The format is designed so software on different computer systems can exchange compressed data. It restores the original bytes and processes a stream without needing storage proportional to the entire stream.

sections.title: The zlib Header and Dictionary Identifier
sections.content:
A zlib stream begins with two bytes: CMF and FLG. For the DEFLATE method, CM is 8 and the window size can be up to 32K; CM value 15 is reserved. The FCHECK bits make the 16-bit value formed from CMF and FLG a multiple of 31.

If FDICT is set, a four-byte DICTID follows. It is the Adler-32 checksum of a preset dictionary, which the compressor and decompressor must both use. The RFC does not specify dictionary contents because suitable dictionaries depend on the application.
sections.plainLanguage: The first two bytes identify the compression method and include a check on the header. A flag can indicate that the stream uses a preset dictionary, whose identifier follows the header.

sections.title: Compressed Data and Adler-32
sections.content:
After the header and any dictionary identifier comes the compressed data. With CM = 8, the data uses the DEFLATE format. The stream ends with a four-byte ADLER32 checksum calculated over the uncompressed data, excluding dictionary data. Bytes after this checksum are not part of the zlib stream.

Adler-32 maintains two sums for each byte: s1 adds the bytes and s2 adds the successive s1 values. Both sums are computed modulo 65521; s1 starts at 1 and s2 at 0. The checksum is s2*65536 + s1, stored most-significant byte first.
sections.plainLanguage: The stream ends with a checksum of the recovered data, not the compressed bytes. A decoder can compare that value with its own calculation to detect corruption.

sections.title: Compressor and Decompressor Requirements
sections.content:
A compliant compressor must produce correct CMF, FLG, and ADLER32 values. It need not support preset dictionaries. If the surrounding format does not use dictionaries, the compressor must not set FDICT.

A compliant decompressor must check the header and checksum and give an error indication if they are incorrect. It must reject a compression method not defined by this version and reject an unknown dictionary identifier when FDICT is set. A decompressor may ignore the FLEVEL hint.
sections.plainLanguage: The compressor must write valid header fields and a checksum. The decompressor must check them and report invalid values instead of silently accepting them.

sections.title: Data Corruption Risk
sections.content: The security considerations state that a decoder that fails to check ADLER32 may allow data corruption to go undetected. The compliance section therefore requires a conforming decompressor to check the checksum and report an error if its value is incorrect.
sections.plainLanguage: If a decoder skips the checksum, it may not notice that the recovered data was corrupted. Checking the checksum lets it report that problem.

fields.name: CINFO
fields.desc: For DEFLATE, describes the LZ77 window size.

fields.name: FCHECK
fields.desc: Check bits making CMF*256 + FLG a multiple of 31.

fields.name: FDICT
fields.desc: Indicates that a dictionary identifier follows.
